title: Dual Laser Triangulator
subtitle: Compact dual-line optical surface profiling
summary: I am building an ESP32-S3 and OV9281 module that measures printed surfaces from two projected laser lines and reports profiles over CAN bus.

content.body: I designed the instrument as a small printer-side measurement system rather than a general-purpose camera. The monochrome sensor observes both laser traces, while the local processing path reduces the captured strip into geometry useful to the printer.

The practical requirement was not simply to see a laser line. I needed a compact head that could acquire two lines, reduce the image locally and return useful surface data without sending a full camera stream through the printer.

I treated the camera, illumination, processing and communication as one instrument. That forced the optical geometry and the PCB outline to develop together: moving a laser or connector by a few millimetres could solve one routing problem while creating an alignment problem elsewhere.

content.body: The PCB combines camera power sequencing, the parallel image interface, laser control and the CAN transceiver within the mechanical limits of the optical assembly.

The sensor interface created the densest part of the board. Ten data lines plus timing, configuration and power sequencing had to stay readable enough to debug, so I kept test access and rail enables even when a smaller schematic would have looked tidier.

The camera I/O voltage also needed deliberate treatment. I checked the exposed module connections instead of assuming that every OV9281 board used the same rail arrangement, then designed the power domains around the actual FFC rather than a generic sensor diagram.

Optical alignment remains the main unknown. The electronics can prove that a frame arrived and a laser switched, but only a calibration target can show whether the two views produce consistent geometry across the required working distance.

title: Gigaplex
subtitle: A complete game console in a 15 × 11 matrix
summary: I designed a CR2032-powered keychain console with a charlieplexed display, five buttons, motion input and sound.

content.body: I reduced the interface to hardware that remains understandable at very low resolution: 165 LEDs, directional controls, one confirmation button and physical motion. The result is small enough to live on a keychain without turning every game into the same blinking square.

The design started with a severe interface budget: a 15 × 11 display, five buttons, a buzzer and motion sensing, all in roughly 35 mm square and powered from a coin cell. Every menu and game mechanic therefore had to earn its pixels and its current draw.

The matrix is charlieplexed rather than driven by a large display IC. That saves board area, but it moves complexity into scanning, brightness control and pin-state safety; one careless output state can light the wrong path through several LEDs.

items.body: Directional buttons handle exact input, while tilt, shake and rotation give the IMU a reason to exist in games such as the sand simulation and dice mode.

items.body: Display scanning, button polling, game updates and buzzer timing were separated so a slow game routine cannot leave the matrix flickering or a note stuck on.

content.body: The firmware architecture separates matrix scanning, input polling, game state and buzzer timing so the tiny MCU can keep the display stable while games and IMU-driven effects run.

The menu was harder than the games. At this resolution two icons that look distinct on a monitor can merge after the real LED pitch, diffusion and viewing distance are considered, so I repeatedly simplified silhouettes and increased empty space.

Memory is another design constraint rather than a late optimisation. Frame data, games and audio must share a small MCU, which is why the video experiments use compact row and delta commands and a deterministic integer-only decoder.

The coin cell cannot be treated like a bench supply. The scan pattern and brightness levels need to limit instantaneous load while still making a partially lit frame look stable, especially when the buzzer or IMU is active at the same time.

title: Code-Less Dice
subtitle: Electronic randomness without a microcontroller
summary: I built an electronic die whose vibration-triggered 555 oscillator cycles six shift-register states before slowing to a stop.

content.body: A brief contact from the vibration switch charges the timing capacitor and starts the roll. The 555 initially clocks the state circuit quickly, then the rate falls with the capacitor voltage until one of the six LED patterns remains visible.

I wanted the behaviour to be visible in the circuit itself. A vibration does not wake firmware or request a random number; it injects energy into an analogue timing network, and the falling clock rate is both the animation and the stopping mechanism.

The six die faces are encoded as hardware states. While the oscillator is fast they blur into a roll, then the slowing clock makes the sequence readable before it settles on the state present at the final transition.

content.title: From a vibration pulse to one held face

items.title: Store the trigger energy
items.body: A momentary contact from the vibration switch charges a capacitor, turning a brief mechanical shock into a timing event long enough to run the roll.

items.title: Generate a decaying clock
items.body: The 555 timer starts at a rapid rate and slows as the stored voltage changes, producing the visible deceleration without any programmed delay table.

items.title: Cycle six display states
items.body: The clock advances the state circuit through the six valid pip patterns rather than allowing electrically convenient but invalid LED combinations.

items.title: Hold the last transition
items.body: When the oscillator stops, the state remains latched so the die shows a stable result until another vibration starts the cycle.

items.title: Initial build
items.body: I selected an HX 0805-C2 believing it was a passive vibration contact, but it was a tilt sensor that required active interpretation and could not trigger the circuit as intended.

items.title: Vibration-switch redesign
items.body: I replaced it with an SW-58010PZD-7N11S1 spring-contact vibration switch and formed its through-hole leads so the part could be mounted flat on the board.

content.body: The first failure came from trusting a part description too quickly. The HX 0805-C2 behaved as a tilt sensor that needed active interpretation, not the passive contact closure required by the analogue trigger circuit.

The replacement SW-58010PZD-7N11S1 had the right spring-contact behaviour but the wrong mechanical format. I bent and trimmed its through-hole leads so the cylindrical body could sit flat and behave like a surface-mounted part.

The stopping action needed tuning as well as randomness. If the clock falls too quickly there is barely an animation; if it falls too slowly the result feels predetermined by a long, repetitive sequence. The capacitor and timing resistance set that character directly.

The finished circuit now reacts to a shake, visibly decelerates and holds one of six valid faces without software. The interesting part is not that a 555 can blink LEDs; it is that the energy from the user's movement shapes the whole interaction.

Because the standard components can be placed by machine, the only unusual production step is forming and soldering the vibration switch. That makes the final revision practical to reproduce rather than a one-off breadboard demonstration.

title: Lumen PnP Feeders
subtitle: Common hardware across four tape widths
summary: I redesigned the 16 mm and 24 mm LumenPnP feeders around the same hardware and electronics used by the 8 mm and 12 mm versions.

content.body: The open-source feeder family originally left the wider sizes with a different assembly burden. I adapted their mechanics so all four widths can share the proven smaller-feeder electronics and as much common hardware as practical.

The wider 16 mm and 24 mm feeders were not merely scaled versions of the smaller units. Their separate architecture increased the number of hardware variants I would need to source, assemble and maintain.

My redesign keeps the open-source feeder's drive and peel functions but adapts the wider mechanics around the electronics and common parts already used by the 8 mm and 12 mm versions. The benefit is mostly operational: fewer unique assemblies, fewer spares and fewer ways to build the wrong board.

I also kept assembly access in mind. A perfectly compact CAD model is unhelpful if the motor screws, connector or tape path become inaccessible once the two halves are printed.

title: Filament Scale
subtitle: A standalone spool station with identity and history
summary: I built an ESP32-S3 filament scale that combines load-cell measurement, NFC spool binding, local records and Spoolman integration.

content.body: I wanted spool tracking to remain useful even when the printer or network was unavailable. The device therefore performs the weighing and identification locally, records transactions to removable storage and can synchronise with an existing Spoolman installation.

I wanted the scale to be a station rather than a peripheral. A spool can be identified, weighed and recorded at the device even if the printer is busy or the network is unavailable, while network services add synchronisation instead of basic functionality.

That choice shaped both the electronics and the interface. The display and three buttons handle routine operations locally; the browser is reserved for configuration, network setup and the larger data views that are awkward on a 240-pixel square.

Early weight readings moved more than the mechanical system justified. I traced part of that behaviour to the HX711 connection and part to an averaging window that was too short, so electrical integrity and filtering were treated as separate problems.

The display also looked wrong until the exact controller settings were found. Rotation alone was not enough; SPI mode, colour format, inversion and memory-access order all affected whether a nominally correct frame appeared with correct colours.

Network configuration created a different class of failure. Switching between station and access-point modes, refreshing the browser status and returning from failed operations all needed explicit states so the interface did not appear to succeed while the device had quietly fallen offline.

title: Smart Reflow Oven
subtitle: Repeatable reflow control with a platinum RTD
summary: I converted a reflow oven to use PT100 temperature feedback after an NTC-based approach proved too sensitive to drift.

content.body: The first sensing approach made calibration too dependent on thermistor behaviour at reflow temperatures. I changed the final design to a PT100 so the controller could work from a more stable and repeatable resistance curve.

The first version could heat an oven, but useful reflow depends on knowing the board temperature well enough to repeat a profile. An NTC that changes behaviour with mounting, calibration and high-temperature drift made the controller look more precise than the measurement actually was.

I changed the final sensing chain to a PT100 platinum RTD. The point was not to chase an impressive decimal place; it was to make calibration and repeated high-temperature cycles behave consistently enough that profile tuning meant something.

content.body: Changing sensor technology did not remove thermal lag. The RTD still needs a repeatable attachment and representative location; otherwise a very accurate sensor faithfully measures the wrong part of the oven.

The cooling segment also matters. Heater power can be reduced instantly, but the chamber and tray retain energy, so the profile logic must anticipate overshoot instead of waiting for the measured peak before reacting.

I treated profile plots as debugging records, not decoration. A run is useful when it shows the target, actual temperature and phase boundaries together, including the parts where the oven cannot follow the ideal curve exactly.

title: Chroma Klipper
subtitle: Printer-side coordination for full-colour FDM
summary: I am developing the Klipper integration that coordinates ordinary print motion with colour output from the ChromaDye hardware.

content.body: This layer turns slicer output into printer behaviour. It has to keep colour deposition aligned with the same motion, timing and state transitions that already govern the underlying FDM print.

A colour-aware slicer and a working cartridge driver are still two separate demonstrations until the printer can coordinate them with motion. Chroma Klipper is the layer that turns colour output into part of the print state rather than an unrelated stream running beside it.

I am keeping this integration narrow. It should translate the slicer's colour plan into timed device actions, expose enough state to diagnose alignment and leave ordinary Klipper motion behaviour intact wherever colour is not involved.

content.title: System position
content.description: The integration sits between colour-aware slicing and the physical deposition controller.

content.body: The main difficulty is ownership of time. The slicer knows where colour belongs geometrically, Klipper owns motion scheduling and ChromaDye owns the final nozzle waveform; none of those clocks can be allowed to drift into an independent interpretation of the print.

A second issue is recovery. Pauses, restarts and empty queues must not resume with colour data offset from extrusion, so the integration needs explicit checkpoints rather than assuming that every print runs uninterrupted from byte zero.

I am resisting the temptation to hide device problems in increasingly clever host code. If the cartridge path cannot accept data deterministically, the correct fix belongs in ChromaDye before Chroma Klipper compensates for it.

title: Chroma Slicer
subtitle: Colour-aware slicing from textured model to layer data
summary: I extended OrcaSlicer with a working full-colour pipeline for textured model import, colour-preserving geometry and per-layer raster generation.

content.body: Colour information normally disappears long before a conventional slicer produces toolpaths. I added a surface representation that keeps UV and texture data attached to model volumes so later stages can ask what colour belongs at each sampled point.

A conventional slicer is very good at reducing geometry to paths, but textured colour is usually discarded before those paths are generated. My first task was therefore preservation: keep the relationship between triangle, UV coordinate and texture alive inside the model instead of trying to reconstruct it after slicing.

I built the work as an OrcaSlicer fork so the colour pipeline sits beside mature mesh repair, slicing and preview behaviour. That also means every new data structure must survive existing transformations without making non-colour projects less reliable.

title: ChromaDye
subtitle: Timing-critical colour deposition hardware
summary: I built the ESP32-S3 cartridge driver that converts colour data into constrained HP123 nozzle pulses for the full-colour printer.

content.body: The controller queues nozzle data and emits a parallel waveform whose pulse widths must stay inside the cartridge limits. The electrical interface is only half the problem; the same timing guarantees have to survive buffering, transfer and printer integration.

An inkjet cartridge is an unforgiving actuator. The driver has to provide the required supply domains and select many nozzles quickly, while also guaranteeing that no software stall can leave a firing pulse active long enough to damage the heater.

I therefore split the problem into waveform generation, buffered transport and physical integration. Each layer can look correct alone and still fail at the boundary, which is why most of the diary is about proving where data stops rather than repeatedly changing the whole design.

content.body: The most misleading failure produced one initial transfer and then silence. Because there was no obvious exception, I had to distinguish an ISR that never ran, a queue that emptied, a DMA descriptor that was invalid and a peripheral that had never been started correctly.

Porting the output was not a name-for-name driver replacement. Buffer ownership, callback signatures, maximum transfer size and the meaning of a completed transaction all changed, so I added explicit size and GPIO checks before allowing data into the hardware path.

Power testing was handled cautiously because cartridge faults can draw real energy. I separated logic, boosted supplies and the attached cartridge during bring-up so a wiring mistake would not be diagnosed by the traditional smell-based interface.

title: Parametric EPaper Dashboard
subtitle: A JSON-composed image pipeline for low-power displays
summary: I wrote a Python and Pillow renderer whose JSON configuration assembles calendar, weather and other modules into one e-paper-ready image.

content.body: Instead of fixing the dashboard layout in one script, I made each section a module that reads its parameters from JSON, renders onto a transparent layer and composes itself onto the shared canvas.

A fixed dashboard script becomes difficult to reuse as soon as the display size, calendar mix or information priority changes. I moved those decisions into JSON so the renderer describes a composition rather than one hard-coded screen.

Each module receives its own parameters and data, renders onto a transparent Pillow layer and returns that layer to the shared canvas. Calendar and weather sections can therefore change independently while the final output remains one image for the display.

I built the reader around the simplest useful desktop interface: a keyboard. When a tag is scanned, the device formats its UID and types the characters into the field that already has focus.

title: Custom Tool Changer

summary: I designed a custom printer that mechanically exchanges five CAN-connected direct-drive tools, each with its own heater and extruder motor.
